```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.align = "center",
                     out.width = "100%", dev.args = list(bg = "white"))
```

When does a zebra travel, forage or rest? We use the GPS track of one plains
zebra in Hwange National Park, Zimbabwe, and the rules proposed by
[Bouderbala, Nicosia and Fortin (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0360547).
The package includes 6,377 observed steps, each 30 minutes long. Gaps separate
the track into 28 segments.

The original tracking study is [Michelot et al. (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1111/biom.13170).
Simon Chamaillé-Jammes provided the GPS track and vegetation raster used in
the [Klappstein et al. archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7872602),
distributed under CC BY 4.0.

## Fit the models

The prepared data give each step's length and turning angle, along with the
direction to the nearest grassland cell from the start of the step. This
makes the target available before the zebra moves.

```{r fit}
library(behavSSF)

zebra <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "hwange-zebra-steps.rds",
                            package = "behavSSF"))
steps <- prepare_ssf_steps(zebra, density_measure = "area",
                           time = "time", expected_interval = 1800)

result <- fit_guided_ssf(
  steps, convention = "area", target = "cos_diff_theta_to_target",
  normalization = "exact", n_starts = 8, short_iter = 100, long_iter = 900,
  seed = 1729
)
result
```

With the default taxonomy, the function first tries habitat-directed
travelling (HDT), foraging and resting. The travelling state must have
the longest mean step and more concentrated turns than the foraging state.
For the HDT label, the 95% confidence interval for the travelling state's
grassland coefficient must lie above zero. If that model fails its checks,
the function tries travelling, foraging and resting without a grassland
term, then travelling and encamped, and finally a single state. It stops
at the first model that passes.

## Read the labels

The article reported habitat-directed travelling, foraging and resting.
Its archived code chose the nearest grassland cell using the observed
step endpoint. Here the cell is chosen at the start of the step, and
the likelihood is integrated directly. In this fit the travelling state's
grassland interval includes zero, so the package selects travelling,
foraging and resting.

```{r step-labels}
overview <- summary(result)
states <- overview$states
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  State = states$state,
  Steps = states$n_steps,
  `Mean step (m)` = round(1000 * states$mean_step),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

The counts come from the Viterbi sequence, which assigns one label to each
step. The means come from the fitted movement distributions.
`overview$candidates` gives the outcome of each candidate that was tried.

## See the states on the track

This map shows the first 48 hours of the longest segment. The open circle
marks where the excerpt starts.

```{r track, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.8, fig.alt="Map of 48 hours of the Hwange zebra track coloured by inferred state. An open circle marks the start."}
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_ssf())
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(bg = "white"))

longest <- names(which.max(table(zebra$ID)))
plot(result, type = "track", segment = longest, step_range = c(1, 96)) +
  labs(title = "48 hours on the zebra's track",
       x = "Relative easting (km)", y = "Relative northing (km)")
```

The probability plot shows how strongly the fitted model supports each state.
When two curves are close, the model gives similar support to the two labels
at that step.

```{r posterior, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.6, fig.alt="Smoothed probabilities of travelling, foraging and resting over the same 96 steps."}
plot(result, type = "posterior", segment = longest, step_range = c(1, 96))
```

## Read the ecological states together

The useful result is a set of states that we can interpret, with the
measurements that support those names. This view brings them together.
Colours follow the labels in every panel. This movement-only fit has no
additional covariates, so the overview omits a coefficient panel. The map uses the same 48-hour
excerpt; the table and distributions use all 6,377 observed steps.

```{r ecological-overview, fig.width=12, fig.height=7.5, fig.alt="Ecological overview combining state counts, the zebra trajectory, step-length and turning distributions with consistent state colours."}
library(patchwork)
plot(result, type = "states", step_scale = 1000, step_unit = "m",
     coord_unit = "km", segment = longest, step_range = c(1, 96))
```

Travelling combines long steps with strong persistence in the previous
heading. Foraging has intermediate lengths and weaker persistence.
Resting has short steps and little directional persistence. These are the
operational meanings of the article's labels at a 30-minute interval.
The GPS data alone do not establish that the animal was feeding or asleep.

The overlaid densities show observed movements grouped by their decoded state.
The distance panel uses a log10 scale with a common smoothing bandwidth.
The circular panel uses `ggcircular`: zero means straight ahead, and 180
degrees means a reversal. Its bandwidth is shared by all states.
They help read the classification, but do not independently validate it.
Means and SDs in the table come from the fitted intrinsic movement kernel;
they are not the empirical means of those groups. The stay probability
and expected run length describe the fitted transition model.

To export the table, use `ssf_state_summary(result, step_scale = 1000,
step_unit = "m")`. For a separate figure, use `plot_ssf_states(result,
panel = "distributions")` or `panel = "coefficients"`. These functions also
work with a fitted model and an accepted custom taxonomy assessment.

## Change the step-length distribution

The same labels can be applied to different movement models. Here we give
the three states names based on their mean step length. The labels describe
the lengths estimated by the model at the 30-minute sampling interval.

```{r length-families}
length_regimes <- ssf_taxonomy(
  "length_regimes", c("Short", "Intermediate", "Long"),
  formula = ~ cos_angle + cos_diff_theta_to_target
)
length_fit <- fit_guided_ssf(
  steps, convention = "area", taxonomies = list(length_regimes),
  step_family = "weibull", normalization = "exact",
  n_starts = 8, short_iter = 100, long_iter = 900, seed = 1729
)
summary(length_fit)
```

Use `step_family = "gamma"` to fit the same taxonomy with a gamma
distribution. The other choices are `"lognormal"`, `"inverse_gaussian"`,
`"halfnormal"` and `"exponential"`. The family supplies the length
distribution, so the formula gives the turning and target terms. To add
vegetation at the endpoint, use case-control rows with that covariate on
both used and available endpoints and choose importance normalisation.

The track and habitat raster come from the article's
[Figshare supplement](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34077912.v2).
The original GPS data are also available in the
[archive of Klappstein, Thomas and Michelot](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7872602).

To compare different numbers of states with your own labels and ecological
rules, see [Choose the number of states with your own taxonomy](zebra-state-count.html).
